newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq seals return as Gulf oil marketing force.
newsitem.headline: Iraq seals return as Gulf oil marketing force.

text.p: Iraq has sealed its return as a marketing force in the oil-rich Gulf by exporting a second supertanker from its Mina al-Bakr terminal under a United Nations "oil-for-food" deal, industry sources said on Thursday.
The 272,000 deadweight tonne Leonidas tanker moved through the Gulf on Thursday following in the wake of the Star Africa tanker which left the al-Bakr terminal on Tuesday.
More tankers filled with Iraqi crude are scheduled to leave the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in the coming days.
"It (Leonidas) left at 1100 local time," said a shipping source in radio contact with the offshore terminal which is 12 miles (19 km) from the southern Fao Peninsula.
Iraq's first customers in the Gulf are both American firms despite Washington's leading role in the allied military effort which expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991.
The two cargoes were set to go to a Caribbean tourist and trading island far removed from Baghdad's austere streets, Western trading sources said.

Texas-based Coastal Corp and independent trading firm Bayoil are expected to take the two cargoes to the tiny Caribbean nation of Aruba in the Netherlands Antilles, close to the South American coast, traders said.
Coastal Corp, led by flamboyant oilman Oscar Wyatt, bought a 205,000 barrels per day (bpd) refinery on Aruba in 1989 which was specially geared up to run off Iraqi crude.

Just months after Coastal's multi-million dollar purchase the refinery's feedstock was swiftly severed when the United Nations slapped an embargo on the export of Iraqi crude when Iraqi forces invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Since then Coastal has kept close ties with Baghdad, highlighted when Wyatt met President Saddam Hussein in December 1990 to negotiate the release of U.S. hostages.

Iraq's rediscovered Caribbean marketing outlets are unlikely to worry Iraq's oil powerhouse neighbours Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iran who are benefiting from windfall petrodollar earnings as prices hold close to post-Gulf War highs.
Even at the height of Iraq's export programme under the U.N. deal, Baghdad's sales are expected to be below 600,000 bpd which represents less than one percent of total world supply.
"The Saudis and the Kuwaitis don't feel squeezed in anyway by these exports...The exports have been absorbed smoothly back into the market," said a Western oil executive in the Gulf.

Most of Iraq's exports are expected to go to Europe through the Ceyhan terminal -- which exported Iraq's first export cargo in six years on December 16 -- and from a pipeline linking the Red Sea to the Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir.
That first cargo was bought by Turkish refiner TUPRAS.
Under the U.N. deal, Iraq is permitted to export $2 billion of its oil over six months on a renewable basis in exchange for food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies.
Iraq bought at least 100,000 tonnes of French wheat on Thursday using money raised through the deal.
